## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Rādhajātaka* (Ja 145) is a birth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. In Burmese epigraphic and manuscript traditions, such as the illustrated series at Pagan, the work is alternatively titled the *Poṭṭhapāda Jātaka*, named after the younger parrot rather than the elder [Ray 1946].

According to the introductory account (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who was hankering after his former wife; the complete background story is cross-referenced to the *Indriyajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Buddha revealed that women cannot be kept under watch, illustrating the theme with two parrot brothers, Rādha and Poṭṭhapāda, who lived under the care of a brahmin [Fausböll 1877]. After the verse beginning *Na tvaṁ Rādha vijānāsi* was expounded and the four noble truths were declared, the backsliding monk attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the elder parrot Rādha was revealed to have been Ānanda, while the younger parrot Poṭṭhapāda was the Bodhisatta [Ray 1946; Fausböll 1877].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the tale across four languages [SuttaCentral].
